questions.question: Strep pneumonia CAP with MICs as follows: Pen 2; Erythro 64; Clinda 256

parts.text: Is it safe to use penicillin? Why or why not?
B.  What is the mechanism of pen resistance in pneumococcus?
C. What are 2 types of macrolide resistance?
d) What type is present here?

cohort_answer.text:
IV Non-meningitic: ≤2 is susceptible --- can use; Po pen: ≤0.06 µg/mL (same breakpoints as meningitis); Meningitic: pen susceptible is ≤0.06 µg/mL, resistant is ≥0.12 µg/mL
Alteration of target enzymes (PBPs)
Efflux pumps (mef in strep pneumo, mSRA in staph aureus), resistance to macrolides, not clinda (M phenotype); Target site alteration by methylation of ribosome to prevent drug binding, resistance to both macrolides, lincosamides, streptogamins (MLSB)
Target site alteration MLSB

questions.question: Practical station: Strep pneumo (CSF).

parts.text: Read Etest for pen and ceftriaxone
How would you report the above MIC's (pen 0.5, ceftriaxone 0.06)?

questions.model_answer:
a) Etest reading: read the MIC at the point where the elliptical zone of inhibition intersects the graduated strip for each antibiotic (penicillin and ceftriaxone).
b) Using the meningitis-specific (CSF) CLSI breakpoints (penicillin: susceptible ≤0.06 mcg/mL, resistant ≥0.12 mcg/mL; ceftriaxone: susceptible ≤0.5 mcg/mL, resistant ≥2 mcg/mL): penicillin MIC 0.5 mcg/mL is reported as resistant, and ceftriaxone MIC 0.06 mcg/mL is reported as susceptible.
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific CLSI numeric breakpoint categories are standard clinical microbiology reference knowledge (CLSI M100) supplementing the Mandell narrative.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man is sent to your office to be evaluated for pneumococcal vaccination.

parts.text: Aside from underlying medical conditions, what are 4 items you could obtain on history to assess his risk for invasive pneumococcal infection?
You decide he is a candidate for the vaccine because he has nephrotic syndrome. Name the vaccine regimen you would use for him, including time intervals and specific vaccine type.

questions.model_answer:
a) History items to assess invasive pneumococcal disease risk (aside from underlying medical conditions): smoking status, alcohol use disorder, residence in a long-term care facility or other chronic-care institution, and social factors such as homelessness/crowded living conditions or Indigenous ethnicity (higher incidence populations).
b) For nephrotic syndrome (an immunocompromising condition), give a conjugate pneumococcal vaccine (PCV13, or PCV15/20 where available) first, followed by PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later; a single revaccination with PPSV23 is given 5 years after the first PPSV23 dose.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI/Canadian Immunization Guide pneumococcal vaccine recommendations for immunocompromising conditions.

questions.question: Pneumococcal pneumonia with pen MIC of 2 and high MICs for clinda and eryth.

parts.text: What is the mechanism of pen resistance?
Can pen be used here?
What is mechanism of macrolide resistance?
Which mechanism in play here?

cohort_answer.text: Penicillin: Mechanism of resistance: altered enzyme structure (PBP) with reduced affinity for the antibiotic. Can be used if IV completely (MIC ≤2). If oral (or CNS infection), cannot use it. Macrolides and Clindamycin: Most likely mechanism is ermB (methylation of ribosome binding site). This gives high level resistance to macrolides and clindamycin (MLSB phenotype). Another mechanism of resistance is mefA (efflux pump), which is low level resistance, but this does not generally impact clindamycin

parts.text: What are the indications for pneumococcal vaccination (and appropriate regimens)?

cohort_answer.text: Indications: routine infant/child immunization, catch-up for missed doses, high risk of IPD due to underlying medical conditions, LTC facility residents, adults 65+, high risk lifestyle factors (smokers, alcoholism, homeless), consider for illicit drug users. Regimens: Age >=65 immunocompetent - PPV23 x1 dose; high risk children 2-18 - PCV-13 followed by PPV-23 >=8 weeks later; high risk adults - one dose PPV-23; boosters for high-risk >=5 years after initial; HSCT adults - 3 doses PCV-13 4 weeks apart starting 3-9 months post-transplant, PPV-23 given 12-18 months post-transplant

questions.question: AM 25. Guy 50 years old who has never been vaccinated for pneumococcus

parts.text: a. What 4 things on history to ask about that are (NOT underlying medical conditions) risk factors for diseases (2)
b. He ends up having nephrotic syndrome - how would you vaccinate him? Name the specific formulations and the timing of vaccine (2)

cohort_answer.text: a) Homeless; alcoholism; smoker; PWID (also: male sex, age <2 or >65, opioid use disorder, ethnic background - African/Alaskan native/American indigenous). b) Nephrotic syndrome considered immunocompromising condition: Conjugate pneumococcal vaccine-13 (PPV-13) x1 dose; polysaccharide pneumococcal vaccine (Pneu-P-23) minimum 8 weeks later with booster 5 years after that.

questions.question: PM 4. Strep pneumonia, Fill in the 3 by 2 chart: describe the 2 mechanisms of resistance to macrolides, what are the 2 genes and state whether it includes clindamycin or not (3)

parts.text: Fill in the chart on macrolide resistance mechanisms

cohort_answer.text: Macrolides insert into a pocket of the 23S subunit of the 50S ribosome, attaching at domain V of the peptidyl transferase loop, blocking protein assembly. mefA-encoded efflux pumps: pump that extrudes macrolides, low level resistance MIC<16, affects macrolide resistance only. ermB-encoded methylases: alter the ribosomal binding site, high level resistance MIC>64, MLSB phenotype - inducible resistance to Macrolide/Lincosamide/Streptogramin B (includes clindamycin).

parts.text: What are 4-historical factors that would prompt pneumococcal coverage other than medical co-morbidities?

questions.model_answer: Four historical/epidemiologic factors (aside from medical comorbidities) that increase risk of pneumococcal disease and should prompt pneumococcal coverage: (1) Active or passive cigarette smoke exposure. (2) Chronic alcohol use/alcoholism. (3) Crowded living conditions (e.g., daycare attendance, military barracks, homeless shelters). (4) Low socioeconomic status or specific high-risk ethnic populations (e.g., Indigenous/Aboriginal populations, African-American ethnicity in US cohorts).

questions.question: Q52 (2008). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia with Pen MIC 2 ug/mL, Clinda 0.1, Levo 1, Erythro 16, CTX 1 ug/mL

parts.text: a) Mechanism of penicillin resistance
b) Can you use penicillin for this case? Justify
c) What are the mechanisms of macrolide resistance (general)
d) What mechanism of macrolide resistance in this case?

cohort_answer.text: a) Alteration of PBPs through mutations of PBP genes, particularly PBP2X and PBP1A (mutated genetic material transferred via transformation). b) Yes - for infections other than CSF, MIC<=2ug/mL is considered susceptible for parenteral penicillin. c) Ribosomal methylation (ermB gene, methylates base in 23S rRNA, alters ribosomal pocket); efflux pump (mefA gene). d) mefA gene acquisition (lower level resistance, MIC<=16) as opposed to ermB (high level resistance, MIC>=64).

questions.question:
Q21 (2013 AM)
Strep pneumonia CAP with MICs as follows: Pen (2), Erythro (64), Clinda (256)

parts.text: B) What is the mechanism of pen resistance in pneumococcus?

cohort_answer.text: PBP alteration in binding affinity (PBP2X). Acquired through transformation (acquiring naked DNA from other dying bacteria). [From Mandell's: six PBP enzymes 1A,1B,2A,2B,2X,3; alterations in PBP2B more likely low-level resistance, mutations in PBP2X associated with high-level resistance; pneumococci acquire resistance genes by transformation, e.g. from S. mitis]

cohort_answer.text: ermB – methylates domain V of the 23S rRNA, altering the ribosomal pocket, resulting in high level resistance (>64). mefA – encodes efflux pump that extrudes macrolides, lower level resistance (<16) (speaker notes: erm - MLSb phenotype (inducible))

cohort_answer.text:
Empirical treatment: Ceftriaxone, Vancomycin
Two therapeutic options: Vancomycin plus a third generation Cephalosporin; Meropenem; Moxifloxacin. Give dex with or within 30mins after 1st dose of abx, if strep pneumo/hib, cont for 48hrs
Follow-up test: Repeat LP. CPS statement:

questions.question: A 5 year old child has strep pneumo meningitis what is your empiric management.

parts.text: What is your empiric management?

questions.model_answer: Empiric management for a 5-year-old with (presumed/confirmed) S. pneumoniae meningitis: vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime), to cover for potential penicillin/cephalosporin-resistant pneumococcus, pending susceptibility results; adjunctive dexamethasone is also generally given, ideally 20-30 minutes before or with the first antibiotic dose.

questions.question: A 5 year old child has strep pneumonia meningitis, MIC of 4 to penicillin and 1 to ceftriaxone.

parts.text: What is your empiric management? Empiric treatment for bacterial meningitis, then two treatment regimens after they tell you the susceptibilities

cohort_answer.text: Empiric treatment = vancomycin 60mg/kg/day IV divided q6h + CRO 100mg/kg/day IV divided BID + dexamethasone at time of antibiotic start; can consider addition of rifampin in setting of dexamethasone use (UTD); would repeat LP 24-48 hrs into therapy. With that MIC, two regimens: a) as above; b) moxifloxacin 400mg IV daily (Sanford)

questions.question: Bacterial meningitis

parts.text: What are the empiric options for treatment of pneumococcus based on MIC?

cohort_answer.text: Penicillin MIC (meningitis) <0.06: use penicillin (R: ≥0.12). Ceftriaxone (meningitis) MIC: S ≤0.5: use ceftriaxone. CTX >1: treat with CTX 2g q12h and Vanco 15-20mg/kg q8h. Rifampin added if CTX >2. Duration 10-14 days

questions.question: PM Q13. Bacterial meningitis. What are the empiric options for treatment of pneumococcus based on MIC?

cohort_answer.text: Penicillin MIC (meningitis) <0.06: use penicillin (R >=0.12). Ceftriaxone (meningitis) MIC S<=0.5: use ceftriaxone. CTX MIC>1: treat with CTX 2g q12h and Vanco 15-20mg/kg q8h; add rifampin if CTX>2. Duration 10-14 days.

questions.question: Meningitis in otherwise healthy 45 M

parts.text: What is empiric treatment?
Strep pneumo on culture with Pen MIC 4, CTX MIC 1, what are two treatment options?
What should you do in in follow-up?

questions.model_answer:
a) Empiric treatment for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in an otherwise healthy 45-year-old adult: vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime), plus adjunctive dexamethasone given before or with the first antibiotic dose (ampicillin would be added if Listeria were a specific concern, e.g., age >50 or immunocompromised, which does not apply here).
b) With S. pneumoniae showing penicillin MIC 4 mcg/mL and ceftriaxone MIC 1 mcg/mL (ceftriaxone-nonsusceptible), two treatment options: (1) Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime). (2) Vancomycin plus moxifloxacin.
c) Follow-up: a repeat lumbar puncture at 24-48 hours should be performed to confirm CSF sterilization/clinical response, given the elevated ceftriaxone MIC and use of a combination regimen for a relatively resistant organism.

questions.question: Name the MOST likely infecting organism in the following scenarios:

parts.text: A patient on eculizumab with fever, nuchal rigidity and headache.
An immigrant person who is undergoing rituximab therapy
Therapy for multiple myeloma who presents with cough, dyspnea and a RLL infiltrate
A splenectomized person who had a dog bite 2 hours ago with bullae surrounding the wound

questions.model_answer:
a) Neisseria meningitidis.
b) Reactivation of chronic hepatitis B virus infection (rituximab-induced B-cell depletion carries a high risk of HBV reactivation, particularly relevant in an immigrant from an HBV-endemic region).
c) Streptococcus pneumoniae (multiple myeloma causes hypogammaglobulinemia, predisposing to infection with encapsulated organisms).
d) Capnocytophaga canimorsus (classically causes fulminant sepsis with bullous skin lesions after dog bites in asplenic patients).
questions.beyond_mandell: Parts b-d draw on general ID knowledge of host-specific pathogen risk (rituximab/HBV reactivation, myeloma/hypogammaglobulinemia, asplenia/Capnocytophaga) beyond the Neisseria-specific Mandell chapter.

questions.question:
Q2 (2015, 2013 PM)
Community-acquired meningitis in an otherwise healthy 45M.

parts.text: a) What is empiric tx?
b) Strep pneumo on culture with pen MIC 4, CTX MIC 1, what are two treatments? What if CTX MIC is 2? Give 2 options for tx?
c) What should you do in follow-up?

cohort_answer.text:
a) Vancomycin (35 to 45 mg/kg/day divided into doses every 8 or 12 h) + third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h). Vanco for the possibility of S. pneumoniae with reduced susceptibility to ceftriaxone (MIC ≥2 µg/mL). Steroids: Because CNS infections can be complicated by cerebral edema and increased ICP --> can give steroids. Give just before (20 min) or with the FIRST dose of abx. Improves outcomes in kids w/ H. influenzae type b, and perhaps pneumococcal meningitis, and in adults with pneumococcal meningitis. Once the first dose of antibiotic has been given, starting dexamethasone is no longer advocated by the 2004 IDSA guidelines, but it is recommended based on expert opinion up to 4 hours after starting antibiotics in the 2016 European guidelines and up to 12 hours in the 2016 UK guidelines. Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h if possibility of encephalitis clinically (but not necessary for HSV meningitis).

b) Penicillin: Intermediate susceptiblity 0.1 to 1.0 µg/mL; Highly resistant when higher than 2.0 µg/mL; CLSI breakpoints of 0.06 µg/mL and lower for susceptible, 0.12µg/mL and higher for resistant. Alteration of PBP. Some serotypes specifically: mostly 6, 14, 19 and 23. 3rd gen cephalosporins (Cefotaxime, Ceftriaxone): Resistance with MIC more than 2µg/mL; When 1µg/mL or less, successful treatment with high-dose 3rd gen Cephalosporin. Vancomycin: Usually used with Cephalosporin; Associated with tolerant strains; Need adjunctive dexamethasone to achieve appropriate CSF concentration. Meropenem: Outcomes similar to cephalosporins - possible agent; Not an alternative for pneumococcal isolates highly resistant to penicillin and cephalosporins. Newer Fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin, Gemifloxacin, Gatifloxacin, Garenoxacin): Good in vitro activity; Comparable outcomes when compared with ceftriaxone; Decreased susceptibility, mostly to Levofloxacin. Regimen given: Ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h PLUS vancomycin IV (trough 15 - 20). 2nd Line: Meropenem 2g IV q8h. 2nd line: Moxifloxacin 400 mg PO q24h. For CTX MIC 2: Meropenem; Moxifloxacin.

c) Repeat LP - 36 to 48h of therapy: any patient who is not improving as expected within 48 hours of therapy, or pneumococcal isolate for which the cefotaxime/ceftriaxone MIC is greater than 2.0 µg/mL (this may be especially important for patients who are receiving adjunctive dexamethasone therapy). Hearing screening and neurodevelopmental follow-up. Vaccination for meningococcal + pneumococcus. Post-exposure prophylaxis. No more details on adult follow up anywhere (not in CID, Mandell, uptodate). [Additional notes: Consider vaccination with Prevnar and pneumovax; Hearing screen (in children – developmental followup); Immunoglobulins, HIV serology; For kids – test for Sickle Cell; Duration of tx for pneumococcal meningitis is 10-14 days; Repeat LP (repeat CSF cx) if: No improvement by 48h of tx, 2-3 d after tx start organism found to be resistant, Persistent fever > 8 days without another explanation, Neonatal gram negative meningitis, CSF shunt infections.]

questions.question: Q46 (2010 AM, 2009 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance (fill in the blank table): K. pneumoniae with Meropenem; P. aeruginosa with Meropenem; E faecium with penicillin; E faecalis with high level aminoglycoside resistance; S. pneumoniae with moxifloxacin; S. pyogenes with erythromycin

parts.text: State the mechanism of resistance for each organism/antibiotic pair

cohort_answer.text: K. pneumoniae/Meropenem: Ambler class D oxacillinases (OXAs); acquired class B beta-lactamases (VIM, NDM); Ambler Class A KPCs; reduced expression of OmpK35/OmpK36. P. aeruginosa/Meropenem: downregulated/absent OprD porin with background AmpC; MBLs (VIM, IMP, SPM-1 less common); upregulation of MexA-MexB-OprM efflux (resistant to mero/doripenem but not imipenem). E. faecium/Penicillin: altered PBPs (resistant pbp5 allele). E. faecalis/HLAR: bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6')-IE-APH(2'')-Ia. S. pneumoniae/Moxifloxacin: dual mutations in GyrA and ParC. S. pyogenes/Erythromycin: erm gene (ribosome methylation) - methylase enzymes dimethylate adenine on 23S rRNA of 50S subunit, disrupting MLS binding.
